passage_text:
Researchers studied the effect of two different dosages of a novel anti‑inflammatory drug on joint pain in a randomized controlled trial. A total of 120 patients with osteoarthritis were enrolled and randomly assigned to placebo, Treatment A (low dose), or Treatment B (high dose). Pain scores were recorded on a 0‑10 visual analog scale at baseline and after 14 days of therapy. The following table summarizes the mean pain scores and percent reduction from baseline for each group after 14 days.

| Group          | Baseline Pain | 14‑Day Pain | % Reduction |
|----------------|---------------|-------------|-------------|
| Placebo        | 7.2           | 6.8         | 5.6%        |
| Treatment A    | 7.1           | 4.3         | 39.4%       |
| Treatment B    | 7.3           | 2.9         | 60.3%       |

The researchers concluded that both doses reduced pain more than placebo, with the high dose showing a greater reduction.
table_data:
Group,Baseline Pain,14‑Day Pain,% Reduction
Placebo,7.2,6.8,5.6%
Treatment A,7.1,4.3,39.4%
Treatment B,7.3,2.9,60.3%
stem: Which of the following statements best summarizes the data presented in the table?

options.A: Treatment B produced a greater percent reduction in pain than Treatment A.
options.B: Placebo had the largest percent reduction in pain.
options.C: Both treatments had the same percent reduction in pain.
options.D: Treatment A had a higher baseline pain score than Treatment B.

explanation: Correct: A) Treatment B achieved a 60.3% reduction versus 39.4% for Treatment A. Why the others are wrong: B) placebo had the smallest reduction (5.6%). C) the reductions were 39.4% and 60.3%, not equal. D) Treatment A's baseline (7.1) was lower than Treatment B's (7.3).
trap: Picking the placebo option because its small 5.6% reduction is also listed, rather than comparing percent reductions across groups.

stem: What is the most appropriate control group for this study?

options.A: A group receiving a higher dose of the same drug
options.C: A group receiving a different anti‑inflammatory drug
options.D: A group receiving no treatment at all

explanation: The placebo group serves as a negative control, allowing the investigators to determine whether the observed pain reduction is due to the drug or to placebo effect. A higher dose group would not serve as a control, and a different drug or no treatment would not provide the same baseline comparison.
trap: Choosing no-treatment because it seems the simplest comparison, but it cannot separate the drug effect from the placebo effect.

stem: Calculate the average percent reduction in pain for Treatment A.
explanation: Percent reduction = (7.1 – 4.3) / 7.1 × 100 = 39.4%, as listed in the table.
trap: Using a wrong denominator (for example dividing 2.8 by 4.3 or by 7.3) gives about 35%, not the correct 39.4%.

stem: Which of the following conclusions is NOT supported by the passage and table?

options.A: The high dose is safer than the low dose because it reduced pain more.
options.B: Treatment B reduced pain more than Treatment A (60.3% versus 39.4%).
options.C: The placebo group showed a small reduction in pain (5.6%).
options.D: Baseline pain scores were similar across the three groups (7.1 to 7.3).

explanation: Correct: A) The study reports efficacy only; no safety or adverse-event data are given, so safety cannot be inferred from a larger pain reduction. Why the others are wrong: B) the table shows 60.3% for B versus 39.4% for A. C) placebo pain fell from 7.2 to 6.8, a 5.6% reduction. D) baseline scores were 7.2, 7.1 and 7.3.
trap: Equating greater efficacy with greater safety, although no safety data were reported.

stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

options.A: Mean pain fell by 4.4 points with Treatment B, 2.8 with Treatment A, and 0.4 with placebo.
options.B: The high dose is the safest choice because it reduced pain the most.
options.C: The low dose should be first-line therapy for all patients with osteoarthritis.
options.D: The drug is no better than placebo at relieving joint pain.

explanation: Correct: A) 7.3 − 2.9 = 4.4, 7.1 − 4.3 = 2.8 and 7.2 − 6.8 = 0.4 points. Why the others are wrong: B) no safety data were collected, so safety cannot be concluded. C) a single 14-day trial without safety data cannot establish first-line use. D) both doses reduced pain far more than placebo.
trap: Turning a short efficacy trial into a treatment recommendation or a safety claim that the data do not address.
